To avoid ambiguity, we unify the terminology as follows: •Raw snapshot: a temporal sample of the physical-array received vectorx l(t)∈C M at timet. The number of raw snapshots is denoted byTin (8). •Cyclic-correlation vector(pseudo-snapshot): the redundancy-averaged vectorr α l (τk)∈C Q obtained from the raw vectorized correlationz α l (τk)∈C M2 at lagτ k. •Pseudo-snapshot matrix: the collection ofKprocessed pseudo-snapshots,R α l ∈C Q×K in (18). Throughout the remainder of the paper, “pseudo-snapshot” refers exclusively to the virtual-array observationr α l (τk), and “snapshot” (without qualifier) refers to the pseudo-snapshot countKin the context of the SBL model. To accelerate subsequent sparse Bayesian inference, we compress the pseudo-snapshot matrixX l =R α l ∈C Q×K using singular value decomposition (SVD). Since sources sharing a common cyclic frequency produce nearly rankone cyclic-correlation snapshots, the number of significant singular values is generally far smaller thanKand may even be smaller than the source countN. We therefore adopt a rank-adaptive truncation: for each base station, we retain the smallest numberK l of dominant right singular vectors whose cumulative energy reaches95%of the total, and set the common dimension asK sv = max 1≤l≤L Kl, clamped to the interval[1,min(N,3)]. ProjectingX l onto the dominant subspace yields the reduced-dimensional measurement matrix XSV l =X lVSl ∈C Q×Ksv,(19) whereV Sl ∈C K×Ksv contains theK sv dominant right singular vectors. This reduces the effective snapshot dimension fromKtoK sv, lowering computational complexity while preserving the dominant signal energy. For notational simplicity, in the SBL derivations of Section IV,X l andK denote the compressed quantitiesX SV l andK sv, respectively; if compression is not applied,K sv =K. IV. Localization Identifiability The available identifiability dictates the maximum number of resolvable sources and is critical in underdetermined scenarios. Physical array methods (CADPD, SBL-AOA-local) are limited toM−1. Virtual array subspace methods (DCAMUSIC, CYC-DCA-MUSIC) require spatial smoothing, restricting identifiability toM s −1. In contrast, CSBL-DPD and AG-CSBL-DPD-I bypass spatial smoothing and directly exploit the redundancy-averaged Khatri–Rao manifoldB l = G(A∗ l ⊙A l), whose difference co-array providesQdistinct virtual elements, achieving(Q−1)/2DOFs. For AG-CSBLDPD-II, however, the off-diagonal mismatch correction relies on the complete Kronecker productC l =A ∗ l ⊗A l whose stable pseudo-inversion requires the physical steering matrix Al to have full column rank. This reduces the identifiability toM−1, making AG-CSBL-DPD-I preferable for underdetermined scenarios and AG-CSBL-DPD-II suitable for overdetermined cases where mismatch correction is prioritized. Conclusions We investigated the DPD problem for multiple sources with intermittent emission. Therefore, we derived the deterministic CRB and presented a computationally convenient approximation of the CRB, which is applicable for practical purposes. Furthermore, we proposed DPD approaches based on the data covariance matrices using a low- or high-dimensional optimization. We used the AP technique to solve the high-dimensional optimization by a sequence of low-dimensional optimizations. In simulations, we demonstrated the superior performance of the ML-DPD approach over the CPN-DPD approach. Consequently, the ML-DPD (and AP-DPD) approach offers a tactical advantage for locating sources with intermittent emission. We proposed an iterative DDPD

Problem formulation about direct position determination of coherent sources As denoted in (6), the position parameters of the emitters only appear at the equivalent array response a ̃l (pk, ωi ), so many spectral methods can be employed to estimate the positions [18,19]. For brevity, (6) is rewritten as the vector form rl (ωi, n) = Al (θ, ωi)s(ωi, n) + el (ωi, n), (7) where Al (θ, ωi ) = [αl1  ̃al (p1, ωi ),..., αlK  ̃al (pK, ωi )], s(ωi, n) = [s1(ωi, n),..., sK (ωi, n)], and “ ” is the transpose notation. Considering the coherency defined in (1), the correlation matrix of the transmitted signals in frequency domain can be expressed as E{s(ωi)sH (ωi)} = ββHE{|s0(ωi)|2}, (8) where β = [β1,..., βK ] and ( · )H denotes the conjugate transpose. Note that the rank of E{s(ωi)sH(ωi)} is equal to 1. The coherency exactly reflects on the correlation matrix. It is also worth mentioning that if the transmitting signals were noncoherent, there would be no signals satisfying sk′ (ωi, n) = βsk(ωi, n) for any k′ = k, where β is a complex constant. It means that the correlation matrix E{s(ωi)sH(ωi)} could always keep its rank full. In [18], according to DPD-MUSIC algorithm, all received signals of L receivers are assembled at a central processing unit, written in a simplified form as follows: r(ωi, n) = A(θ, ωi)s(ωi, n) + e(ωi, n), (9) where r(ωi, n) = [r1 (ωi, n),..., rL (ωi, n)], e(ωi, n) = [e1 (ωi, n),..., eL (ωi, n)], A(θ, ωi) = [A1 (θ, ωi),..., AL (θ, ωi)], θ = [p1,..., pK ]. When using the MUSIC approach, the covariance matrix of the received signal r(ωi, n) is required to be computed. That is R(ωi) = E{r(ωi)rH (ωi)} = A(θ, ωi)E{s(ωi)sH (ωi)}AH (θ, ωi) + ηI, (10) where ηI is the covariance matrix related to noise part. Note that as shown in (8), the rank of E{s(ωi)sH(ωi)} is much less than the number of signals K, which can result in the rank-deficient property of R(ωi). DPD-MUSIC algorithm is implemented on the basis of the orthogonality of signal subspace and noise subspace, so it needs to make an eigenvalue decomposition for the covariance matrix R(ωi). However, affected by the rank-deficient covariance matrix R(ωi), only the eigenvectors less than the number of emitters can be obtained. Therefore, it leads to the invalidation of DPD-MUSIC algorithm for coherent signals. The similar consequence also happens in the DPD-MVDR algorithm [19], since the inverse of the covariance matrix is required to be computed when using MVDR approach. The rank-deficient property of the covariance matrix also significantly causes unstable computation of its inverse, which further results in the degradation of the robustness and accuracy of DPD-MVDR for the coherent sources. Next, we will focus our attention on the solution to locate multiple coherent sources.
